Title: Is it Time to Retire Top Cards

Messages.Author: Ben Swainbank
Messages.Body:
All this talk about Voter Captivation, and when cards should and
should not get changed, has reminded me of something I've been
noodling about for while. Very often when I'm thinking about building
decks that include new cards I find myself abandoning them in favor
the old standbys. Grooming the Protege? Eh, Blood Doll is probably
better. Auto-da-fe? Better to stick with KRC.

The same few cards have been dominating game spaces like combat, pool
gain, and politics since the game arrived. This is typical of CCGs -
the first batch contains cards that end up on the very high end of the
power curve. Other long-lasting games have dealt with this via banning
and/or set rotation. I'm not advocating for that.

I would suggest that the old-standbys are constricting design choices
on two levels. Cards shouldn't be introduced that are better than the
old power cards, and there's not much point in designing cards that
are worse. Similarly, for players, you can jump though hoops to try to
gain advantage by doing something new. Or you can play the same cards
we've been playing for 12 years - because they are still the best
there is for doing what they do.

Is it time to kill our darlings? Can we take the top cards, the moldy
oldies, thank them for years of faithful service, extend our gratitude
for the multitude of VPs, and offer then a long overdue retirement?

Banned or nerfed, that's a supplemental debate, I would like to offer
up the following old friends for "the block" - not because they are
broken, or dominate the meta-game (they aren't and don't) - but
because it's time for somebody new.

Kine Resources Contested
Conservative Agitation
Consanguineous Boon
Blood Doll
Torn Signpost
Carrion Crows
.44 Magnum
Direct Intervention
Voter Captivation

Any cards I missed? Anybody else think a little retirement party would
be good for the game?

-Ben Swainbank

I'm all in favor of a retirement party for certain cards, but only
"problem" cards, not cards which are useful and perhaps slightly
powerful.

I wouldn't ban any of the cards on your list, though Carrion Crows and
Direct Intervention are probably the two worst offenders IMO. I'd be
happy if Carrion Crows cost 1 blood because it's environmental damage
and not strike dependent.

While there has been discussion about Voter Cap lately, I still think
it is harder now for vote decks than ever before. There are so many
titles scattered about, especially in Third Edition, that you have to
push very hard to get anything through with 4 opponents (or negotiate
exceedingly well).

Dominate (of course) is the biggest problem in the game. Still. After
13 years. Even after Deflection was reduced in power recently after
that old ruling was dredged up. I think the jury is still out whether
this makes Dominate less powerful (bounce not as good) or about on par
(still the best bleeders). Govern and Conditioning could go and the
game would not be any worse for the wear. It'd just be slightly harder
for Dominate clans to win, but they'd still do well. FYI, 38 of the 91
(41.8%) winners in the latest storyline had Dominate in-clan. I'd
venture several of the other winning decks also featured Dominate-
graft of some sort.

The greatest asset this game has, imo, is the fact that 12 year old
cards are still competitive in the current meta. Credit has to be
given to the design crew in regards to the care they've taken in that
respect. In every other CCG I've played, rotation is almost always the
straw that breaks the camel's back.

I don't believe those old cards are restricting design. I believe the
devs are more than capable of taking the game in new and interesting
directions, and they've demonstrated that there's still plenty of
fertile territory within the WoD paradigm. However, I believe LSJ and
co are, probably for the very reasons stated above, too conservative
in introducing new concepts for fear of blowing the power curve, with
the result that these new concepts/strats are simply dismissed out of
hand by the majority of the player base, and they just go back to the
trusty ol' SB/ConsAgg merry-go-round.

Best example of this, to my mind, is KMW, and the concepts of Red List
and Trophies. Very cool idea, had the potential to give combat a big
boost, but due to the added complication of including a red list/
trophy module in already crowded and card thirsty combat decks for
what is to my mind [and many others, apparenly] far, far too little
return from the Trophies [a Hunting ground - wow....] the whole
concept seemed to fall quite flat.

The new ideas and concepts are already there. The last few years have
given us Red List/Gehenna/Hunters/Anarchs. I think the design team
have already demonstrated they're capable of thinking of the ideas,
they just need to be a little braver in their implementation, imo.

That's because you're a good deckbuilder and you use the best available
options. There are a few exceptions of course. But the new options are
generally spice, not meat and potatoes.

In the past, what had profound impact on our deckbuilding? For me, it was
Bloodlines. Lots of new options to explore, with lots of shiny new
discipline-based toys to sprinkle in with all the staple cards. A
competitive deck or two even came out of that set (Ahrimane wall, Turbo
Baron, Kiasyd-Lasomba combo).

Since then.....Anarchs.....Black Hand......Abombwe. Each of which have
limited playability compared to the older, tried and true archetypes and
certainly lack the depth that 13 years of published card options provide.

mind.

> old power cards, and there's not much point in designing cards that
> are worse.

other games have seen.....but it sure makes it tough to get excited about

library cards until I've parsed all the new crypt cards - that's where the
potential usually lies.

Messages.Body:
Another voice here rallying against set rotation and dropping of old
cards.

It is an impressive achievement that after 12 years not only is every
set still legal for play, but that all the critical cards are kept in
print and available to new players. Regarding the power level, I
really dont think that the original Jyhad cards were overpowered.
Jyhad was the single best and most balanced set to ever come out for
the game. It is the benchmark on which all else has been done, and
rightly so. Sets like Bloodlines and Final Nights were fantastic
because they added very playable clans (or corrected the problem with
old clans) in very very elegant ways that didnt in any way change how
the game was played. Less competitive sets like Anarchs or KMW are
still waiting for some expansions to do to them what Final Nights did
to Dark Sovereigns and Ancient Hearts. Removing those original cards
or sets to make the more recent additions balanced would be a
mistake. The solution is to bring forward better balance with ffuture
expansions.

What you can do however, is identify individual cards released since
Jyhad that have dramatically affected how games are played. I think
Carrion Crows was one definite such card. I remember first seeing
that card and shaking my head in disapproval. If the effects only
lasted for the round instead of the whole combat it would have been
more balanced, but as it was it was essentially free environmental
damage the equivalent of 2 murder of crows on your vamp, only without
the blood cost or the time to recruit factor. Immediately you saw
weenie decks with aid from bats and Carrion Crows popping up, and
recent cards like Pack Alpha have only barely begun to reverse some of
the effects that single card had on how the game is played.

The most recent addition to dramatically change the game was Mirror
Walk IMO. There is a card that simply should not have been printed
(the superior version at least). Way to change the Tremere from a
clan that required serious thought and discipline in deck building
into mindless and fearless forward bleeders. Whereas cards like
Telepathic Tracking and Wind Dance were exactly the kind of thing the
clan needed, Mirror Walk was just overkill. It really should have
been a little less powerful (more along the lines of Stealth Ritus).

It is these crucial cards that appear here and there that should be
seriously evaluated. My main concern with the game has been that
slowly disciplines are beginning to resemble each other more and
more. Intercept for celerity? Stealth for thaumaturgy? Discipliness
intercept and stealth? Abbot??? More and more decks begin to
resemble each other. The day we see discipliness bleed redirection
cards is the day the game will finally jump the shark (like a Gangrel
who can redirect bleeds, who would have thought that would ever happen
5 years ago?).

should have the capacity to defend against it. It occurs with all

matter of power, it's a matter of votes not working in a way that
allow a legitimate defence.

Not a good idea for two reasons. One is backward compatibility - many

No, I don't think there's time for such newness. If there is waning

I'm not sure how gutting the game would benefit the player base. There's
a good deal of controversy in where VtES is headed anyway; I'm all for
radiating some tranquility and reliability towards the player base.

If I were a designer, I'd strengthen VtES through the following points:

- Card Quality Assurance - make sure all cards are visually designed,
and printed in a quality way. Have someone check for typos, art
inconsistency and printed card quality.

- Tournament Incentive - instead of pissing off players by printing
truckloads of legendary card promos that a lot of players never see
regardless of tournament attendance I'd think of a system to ensure
that whatever incentive is used to lure players in for the tournaments
are really reaching them (2006 Qualifier T-Shirts anyone?).

- Enforce card versatility - there are dozens of fractions and
requirements in the game. Disciplines, clans, sects, special
descriptors - you name it. I see countless non-mainstream
opportunities there, like powerful multi-discipline effects, solid
clan-based cards, power-up for underdog concepts (Sword of Caine
looks promising in this respect).

- Coherence in design - I'd steer clear of fumbles like NoR, and
rather innovate within some accepted boundaries. I, for one, would
love to see some sort of chronological or spatial separation - I've
been pondering ways how regions could be introduced into the game,
like tying certain cards to certain bases of power, or how a special
edition Dark Ages set could be at least partially incorporated into
the game (like, having a separate non-compatible vampire group, and
having the rule in place that DA cards can be used in VtES if the
requirements are met, but not vice verse).

I wouldn't nerf existing cards that do not upset the game one way or
another.

I'm just off a great weekend of V:tes at the NEQ. I've got a lot of
love for the game right now and a bunch of new deck ideas. So, I
should probably point out a few things:

First off, I agree that the game is very well balanced right now.
Walking around at the qualifier this weekend, I'm guessing there were
about 30 different, distinct deck types being played among the
players. Great variety and decks of all shapes and sizes. I don't
think vote, or weenies, or walls or anything is particularly dominant.
In general, V:tes set design has been great and the new sets
consistently introduce new "good" stuff.

Second, I'm a fairly prolific and not very conservative deck builder.
I am always striving to build decks that both new and good. I always
want to play with the new toys. I don't have much interest in making
decks that are tired or that suck. Nor am I excited about playing
against sucky and/or tired decks. But I respect that people should
build and play whatever they want. What seems like old hat to me might
be fresh and fun (or just good) to somebody else. So, I don't complain
much.

So, what's the problem? While there is a great variety and balance in
the game, there is also some stagnation in the top tier. With any deck
I answer the question of "how good is it?" by doing a checklist
against the top types. Can it stop powerbleed? Control breed/boon?
What if Arika is my predator? Weenie vote? Potence rush? That
"benchmark" list has changed a little in the past 10 years, but not
much. Most of the decks that have won Continental Championships could
have been built in previous millennium.

I am against set rotation. But I do have some envy of way the
"rotators" can (are forced to) rediscover and reinvent the game and
the top tier periodically. The downside is that you can pretty much
throw away your old cards. Very bad. I would suggest that the best of
both worlds would be to occasionally take the scalpel to the top 0.1%.
Move the top tier by selectively adding a cost and cutting efficiency
here and there. Move cards from the no-brainer, top of the heap, back
into the position of being a contender fighting for deck space.

This isn't really anything new. The most obvious case was the
Camarilla Edition reprints. Was the game broken when Majesty was free
and you could refill with 5th Tradition? No. But I would argue that
the game is better because those changes were made. In retrospect, the
benefits of those changes outweighed the (admittedly non-trivial)
costs of assimilating them.

I suggest that another wave may be warranted and offer some
candidates. I would even suggest that such changes become part of the
official game balance evolution strategy (we have one right?). Instead
making it a surprise (V:tes players don't seem to like surprises) make
it routine. With every set, change 1 card. Introduce 200 new cards.
Tweak 1 old one. Put it in the preview.

Yes, its change for the sake of change. But very, very slow change...

> The game needs DI as a remedy against "weird" decks
> and strategies,

Right. We wouldn't want any of those "weird" decks creeping into the
game. That would be no fun.

-Ben Swainbank

Intercept decks could use a boost? In what world? Like, yeah, intercept
decks aren't super good at *winning* games, yeah, but that is a good
thing--offense should be better than defense (and generally is in most
parts of this game), otherwise the game grinds down into a defensive
standstill. Currently, you can pretty easily build a reasonably good
intercept deck that can very reliably get 2VPs per game (from being the
last guy left at the table). Which is fine, 'cause if intercept decks
got too good at winning games while being completely defensive, the game
stops being interesting.

> demonstrates how Awe is overpowered. Does the game really needs a card
> that provides +20 votes or more?

Awe isn't overpowered. Awe is perfectly fine. It has a very steep cost
for a strong effect. Most of the time, Awe is simply overkill--if you
have significant table votes, or overlapping non Awe modifiers
(Bewitching+Iron Glare+Scalpel Tongue or whatever). In decks that
*don't* have access to significant table vote weight or overlapping vote
mods (i.e. you are the Settites, say), Awe is a powerful tool that lets
you compete with all the other vote heavy hitters who do have access to
overlapping vote mods. But in the case of, like, Arika/Ventrue Law Firm
kinda stuff, Awe is more often than not just pure overkill. Especially
'cause it is so gosh darn expensive to play (for 1 blood at PRE, Awe is
*less* useful than Bewitching...)

Where Awe becomes a serious enabling factor is in a situation where the
number of votes you win by becomes significant, and when the blood cost
becomes a non factor. Hmm. I wonder what could set up such a situation?

All this is true. Any voting deck should make some deals and be
flexible. But if we assume that there are no intercept decks on the
table, Awe will constantly break the vote balance. For instance,
Player A has 3 votes, Players B and C have 4, and Player D has 2
votes. If player A wants to push his vote, he MUST deal with somebody
to get his/her votes. Even Bewitching won't allow him to push the vote
against the whole table, and that's perfect. The whole votes mechanic
was meant to incorporate the need of such deals. The more permanent
votes you have - the more you can trade for them. Playing large
vampires with a lot of votes is risky, so the players should be
rewarded for the risk.
Awe completely destroys this mechanic. Player A can push any vote
against the whole table, and that's horrible. "My Anneke plays
Alastor. 10 votes against? She plays Awe!" Yes, Awe will cost some
blood, so what? Even without VC Anneke can return that blood with
Taste of Vitae and her new Assault Rifle :) And the most horrible
thing is the fact that she can push such votes several times! Six Awe
and six Alastors are quite logical, and I'm laughing at those Inner
Circles (in fact, I can even push Justicar Retribution and burn them
all!) This situation cannot be considered "normal". Vote mechanics
wasn't meant to be broken so easily.
Restricting Awe to "once per game" would be quite logical.
Alternatively, one could add another restriction... like "X cannot be
less than 3". This would at least prohibit free cycling and lead to
the smaller number of copies in playable decks.

reasonable. Not trying to start up a discussion on Voter Cap again,
but in the Awe+Voter Cap equation, I truly believe that the Voter Cap
is the problematic element, not the Awe.
